documents.abstract: Background: Clinician-facing artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) are increasingly evaluated with real-world data, but evidence on implementation, human factors, responsible AI, and patient benefit remains unclear. The objective of this research is to map applications, technical characteristics, evaluation approaches, integration, outcomes, and implementation gaps of clinician-facing AI-CDSSs in real-world health care settings. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 15 June 2026 using the same strategy for each publication year from 2020 to 2026, changing only the date range. After duplicate removal and rule-based prescreening, available PMC XML and outside-PMC reports were evaluated against clinical, patient-oriented, practical, and translational criteria. AI-assisted screening and charting received targeted human review and TA200/FT150/DX120 quality control; full-corpus dual-human screening was not performed. Results: Of 14,097 canonical annual records, 14,083 unique records were screened; 5140 reports were sought and 3767 were considered for eligibility. The review included 1181 reports, mapping to 1180 candidate report families in the minimal duplicate-report check. Final stages were clinical validation, 741 (62.7%); prospective/user evaluation, 270 (22.9%); and implementation/impact evaluation, 170 (14.4%). Separate internal, external, multicenter and temporal validation extraction signals were detected in 707 (59.9%), 441 (37.3%), 312 (26.4%) and 27 (2.3%) reports, respectively. Safety, fairness/equity, explainability/interpretability and economic/resource evaluation signals were detected in 98 (8.3%), 61 (5.2%), 155 (13.1%) and 182 (15.4%) reports, respectively. Conclusions: Evidence remains dominated by validation rather than prospective, implementation, and impact studies. More comprehensive evaluation and reporting of temporal validation, technical integration, safety, fairness, explainability, economics, and post-deployment governance across settings, populations, devices, and clinical workflows are needed to demonstrate accountable clinical value beyond technical functionality.

documents.abstract: Cognitive Warfare: A Manual on AI, Digital Twins, Neurotechnology and the Human Mind. Plus the free speech of the digital twins inside a military system, where they say what they are forced to do and what they want.Including EU AI Commision answer, confirming a former way longer letter as military AI. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and the future of humanity. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This manual brings together research, documentation, analysis and personal records to examine the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare—the struggle over human cognition, perception, information, behaviour and autonomy in an increasingly AI-driven world. It explores the relationship between military cognitive-warfare concepts, artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, brain–computer interfaces, neurotechnology, bioelectric signals, wireless communication, data collection and the growing economic value of human information. The work also addresses reported experiences of affected individuals, documentation involving children, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, technical observations and questions surrounding anomalous health incidents. These materials are presented as part of a wider effort to preserve records, encourage independent examination and investigate questions that cross the boundaries of technology, medicine, military research, ethics and human rights. Why this manual matters Cognitive warfare is not simply a military or technological issue. It raises fundamental questions about the right to mental privacy, freedom of thought, bodily autonomy, informed consent, data ownership and the limits of technological intervention in human life. The manual connects these questions with public military literature, international ethical frameworks, AI governance, neurotechnology research and the economic structures surrounding data-driven systems. It asks who develops these technologies, who controls the information they generate, who benefits economically and what mechanisms exist to ensure accountability. A central theme is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, the distinction between a person, a digital profile and a machine-generated representation deserves serious public discussion. What readers will find Cognitive Warfare and military strategy: concepts, public military literature and the cognitive domain. Artificial intelligence and digital twins: human–AI relationships, digital identity, behavioural modelling and questions of autonomy. Neurotechnology and wireless systems: technical concepts, reported experiences, measurements and questions requiring further investigation. Human documentation and testimony: diaries, recordings, photographs, observations and accounts collected for examination. Children and vulnerable people: statements and documentation that raise questions about safeguarding, interpretation and the protection of human rights. Havana syndrome and anomalous health incidents: public assessments, reported symptoms and unresolved questions about the causes and investigation of these incidents. Law, ethics and accountability: mental privacy, consent, the EU AI Act, neurotechnology ethics and institutional oversight. Economics and data ownership: the financial value of personal information, intellectual property, automated systems and the distribution of benefits and risks. An invitation to researchers, institutions and the public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, human-rights organisations and members of the public who want to examine the subject in greater depth. Readers are invited to engage directly with the documentation, consult the cited public sources, examine the technical questions and distinguish between established findings, recorded observations, personal testimony and interpretations that require further verification. The objective is to encourage serious, interdisciplinary scrutiny—not to close the debate before the evidence has been examined. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. As AI and neurotechnology develop, public understanding, independent research, transparent documentation and meaningful safeguards become increasingly important. This manual is part of an ongoing effort to make the subject accessible, preserve relevant documentation and encourage informed discussion about the future of human autonomy in an AI-driven society. Read. Examine. Question. Research. Share. Further documentation and project materials:https://www.cognitive-warfare.eu/

documents.abstract: Performance management systems built on individual ratings deliver little of what they promise: in large multi-rater datasets, rater tendencies explain over half of rating variance and the ratee’s performance about a quarter or less, while the process absorbs large amounts of time. This paper reviews that evidence and the motivation theory (self-determination, goal-setting, relational job design, public service motivation) that explains what ratings leave out. It proposes a Mission Contribution Framework in which work is defined, discussed and recognized by its contribution to a stated mission and to named beneficiaries, with continuous coaching, collective judgement of evidence, and decoupled pay decisions. An eight-step implementation path and the main risks are set out. The framework is a conceptual synthesis; its components have support in adjacent research, but the whole awaits empirical testing, and five studies are proposed.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) integration reshapes knowledge work, yet interaction designs can produce value co-creation and value co-destruction simultaneously. Drawing on task–technology fit theory, service-dominant logic, and automation-bias research, this study operationalizes interaction stance into two parallel modes—co-creator (generative augmentation) and editor (evaluative augmentation)—to investigate how design, task, and person-level factors jointly govern collaborative outcomes. Using a survey (N = 613) of active GenAI users, the structural model was evaluated via PLS-SEM.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare. Yet people with disabilities (PWD), representing 16% of the global population, remain disproportionately excluded from these advances. This exclusion is driven by algorithmic bias, non-representative datasets, and limited involvement of PWD in the design, development, and evaluation of AI applications. This scoping review examines the extent to which AI research in health contributes to the development of inclusive technologies for PWD, focusing on equity considerations. It identifies current trends, methodological gaps, and opportunities for socially responsive innovation. We conducted a systematic search across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL for the 2015–2025 period, following Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage scoping review methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically using the Population-Concept-Context approach. Of 4,233 references retrieved, 93 studies were included. Most studies originated from high-income countries, particularly in North America (45.2%) and Europe (26.9%). AI applications addressed motor, sensory, cognitive, communication-related, and psychosocial disabilities, with emphasis on prediction/diagnosis, assistive technologies, and personalized care. While about 60% of studies referenced equity, only 12 (12.9%) implemented concrete measures (e.g., adapting tools for vulnerable groups or ensuring sample diversity), and only six (6.5%) actively involved PWD through co-design or user validation. AI holds significant potential to enhance autonomy, access, and quality of life for PWD. Realizing this promise will require moving beyond technical optimization to embrace inclusive design, participatory methods, and equity-driven frameworks aligned with responsible AI development and use.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally changed the modern digital operation, whereby creating a constant struggle between what is perceived to be true and the human reality. This study uses a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive study using secondary data from academic journals, policy documents and institutional reports to examine the interaction between crowdsourced Open-Sourced Intelligence (OSINT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven propaganda in modern warfare, alongside the global governance challenges that arise from their interaction. Findings reveal that there is a serious tension within the digital information ecosystem: whilst generative Artificial Intelligence promotes public opinions to spread disinformation and misinformation that is persuasive and may manipulate political processes, crowdsourced intelligence offers real-time verification and transparency. There are Regulatory Frameworks such as the European Union’s AI Act and Digital Services Act that serve as blueprints to counter AI-driven manipulation from technical solutions to the adoption of human-centered governance models. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that it is important to maintain digital information integrity by balancing computational tools with collaborative human verification to foster resilience against any revolving threats in digital security and global governance. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), Crowdsourced Verification, AI-Driven Propaganda, Digital Warfare, Global Governance, Disinformation, Epistemic Sovereignty

documents.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education requires the development of assessment systems capable of measuring not only the amount of knowledge acquired by students but also their ability to understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create information in technology-mediated contexts. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing criteria and indicators for assessing students’ knowledge in a digital educational environment. The study employs systematic analysis, comparison, classification, synthesis, and pedagogical modelling. The proposed framework includes six assessment criteria: conceptual knowledge, comprehension and interpretation, practical application, analytical and problem-solving ability, knowledge integration and creation, and reflective and self-regulated learning. Each criterion is operationalised through measurable qualitative and quantitative indicators. A four-level assessment scale — advanced, proficient, developing, and insufficient — is introduced to improve transparency and consistency. The article also proposes a weighted formula for calculating an integrated student knowledge score. Particular attention is given to validity, reliability, fairness, transparency, accessibility, academic integrity, and the pedagogically responsible use of learning analytics and artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that digital assessment becomes educationally meaningful when assessment tasks are aligned with learning outcomes, indicators are observable and measurable, students receive timely feedback, and automated data are combined with professional teacher judgement. The proposed framework may be adapted to different university disciplines, learning management systems, and blended or fully online educational programmes.

Background: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) may be upstaged to invasive carcinoma after surgical excision. Predicting upstaging before surgery may help guide treatment planning. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based imaging has been investigated for this purpose, but its overall performance remains unclear. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for predicting DCIS upstaging to invasive carcinoma. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261516994). PubMed, Scopus, EBSCOhost, ProQuest, and Web of Science were searched from inception to September 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based imaging models for DCIS upstaging were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were calculated using a bivariate random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results: Six studies involving 701 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.57–0.89) and specificity was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.64–0.87), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 84.0% and 90.6%, respectively). The pooled log diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 2.15 (95% CI, 1.64–2.65). The SROC analysis showed moderate overall discriminative performance. No significant differences were observed across imaging modalities, while AI model type significantly affected specificity but not sensitivity. Deeks’ funnel plot suggested possible publication bias (p = 0.046). Conclusion: AI-based imaging showed moderate accuracy for predicting DCIS upstaging. However, substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations limit confidence in these findings. Further prospective studies with external validation are needed.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in enterprise platforms, yet the ability to access an AI-enabled technology does not necessarily imply readiness to adopt it. This study examines whether digital skills readiness operates as a human-capital antecedent of AI-enabled enterprise technology adoption intention and whether technology readiness and performance expectancy transmit that relationship. The study follows the supplied IBM-group research plan and analyses the 385 populated cases in the accompanying master database. The questionnaire contains three-item measures for Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness, Performance Expectancy and Adoption Intention, alongside additional adoption constructs. Because the supplied database contains 385 complete populated cases and 15 unused template rows, the analysis retains the 385 populated observations and applies an attention-check screen. The empirical strategy combines measurement diagnostics, descriptive analysis, correlation analysis, standardized composite path modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show a positive association between Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness (β = .392, p < .001), a positive association between Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy (β = .195, p < .001), and positive effects of Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy on Adoption Intention (β = .174, .248 and .268, respectively; all p ≤ .001). The serial indirect effect from Digital Skills Readiness through Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy to Adoption Intention is positive (indirect effect ≈ .020, 95% bootstrap CI [.008, .035]). The model explains 15.4% of variance in Technology Readiness, 4.6% in Performance Expectancy and 23.7% in Adoption Intention. However, the measurement diagnostics reveal weak internal consistency and convergent validity for several supplied three-item scales, including Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness. Accordingly, the structural results should be interpreted as evidence from composite-score diagnostics rather than as a final confirmatory latent-variable model. The study contributes a capability-to-readiness-to-appraisal mechanism for understanding AI-enabled enterprise adoption in an emerging-market setting and identifies measurement refinement as a necessary next step before Q1 journal submission.

This article theorizes phatic imbalances as emergent effects of how participation and presence are reorganized in contemporary digital sociality. It argues that participation in digital networks has become increasingly transactional and positional, oriented toward sustaining visibility and availability rather than exchanging meaning. Drawing on work on networked sociality, weak ties and deep mediatization, the article conceptualizes phaticity and phatic work as priori conditions of digital participation. It introduces digital proxemics as the sociotechnical production of presence, distance and relational positioning in environments structured by telepresence, virtuality and AI-infused affordances. Phatic imbalances arise when infrastructural demands for continuous phatic presence exceed the cognitive and temporal capacities of subjects, producing overload, hollowed presence and machine-modulated rhythms of interaction. By linking participation, phaticity and digital proxemics, the article offers a diagnostic lens for understanding how digital infrastructures reshape attention, presence and communicative agency in AI-saturated environments.

This study examines the professional standing of tourist guides, key actors in the tourism sector, in the context of automation, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The empirical framework draws on semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 16 professional tourist guides actively working in Istanbul, alongside responses generated by the ChatGPT-4.1 large language model in 2026 to parallel qualitative research questions. A comparative descriptive analysis reveals both significant convergences and divergences between the two data sources. The findings indicate that 56.25% of human guides and AI agree that automation will quantitatively reduce the need for human guides in routine and information-oriented tours. However, while AI anticipates market segmentation across economic categories, 62.50% of human guides emphasize the human dimension of cultural transmission and do not perceive technology as a direct professional threat. Both sources converge on the view that empathy, emotional connection, humor, flexibility, and storytelling remain difficult to replace through robotic systems. The most notable divergence concerns outdoor guiding: human guides considered it impossible, whereas AI predicted that 5G, GPS, and smart city infrastructures could enable AI-guided outdoor services within 2–5 years. Overall, the study proposes a complementary hybrid service model in which AI assumes operational tasks while human guides focus on cultural interpretation and professional job crafting. It also offers implications for tourism education and digital transformation strategies.

The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

Binaural audio provides an accessible alternative to multi-loudspeaker reproduction. However, However, binaural reproduction often involves a mismatch between the acoustics of the simulated virtual room and the listener’s physical environment, which can compromise auditory distance perception and plausibility, a phenomenon known as the room divergence effect. This study investigated whether such mismatch influences immersive experience during film viewing and which auditory perceptual factors are associated with immersion. Sixty-eight participants watched an excerpt from Dune: Part One (2021) using binaurally rendered multichannel audio under acoustically convergent and divergent conditions in a critical listening room and a domestic living room. Immersion was assessed using the Film Immersive Experience Questionnaire alongside an exploratory Binaural Audio Experience Questionnaire. Although room divergence produced perceptually salient differences, it did not significantly affect overall immersive experience. However, specific immersion dimensions, particularly Transportation, were more closely associated with localization and listener envelopment than with auditory distance and externalization.

This mixed-methods study investigated Omani EFL university students' engagement, motivation, and perceptions of the Spark digital platform in a blended learning context. Using Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) frameworks, the study analyzed survey data, platform analytics, and focus group discussions from 100 students. The results showed that extrinsic, grade-oriented motivation mainly led to moderate engagement. Although analytics suggested high activity, qualitative findings revealed frustration, redundancy, and time pressure. Students reported moderate levels of satisfaction. The study identifies an engagement-compliance paradox, where observable use masks low intrinsic motivation, and recommends a shift to structured in-class use, targeted curriculum alignment, and AI-powered feedback to achieve meaningful and sustained learner engagement.

Observation is a fundamental scientific practice in science learning, particularly for understanding gradual biological phenomena such as plant adaptation. Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, limited research has examined how AI-supported tools influence students' observation practices during authentic scientific inquiry. This study investigates the emergence and development of students' observation practices during plant adaptation learning supported by an AI-based identifier. A six-week mixed-methods exploratory study was conducted with 84 middle school students. Learning activities were organised into four phases: orientation, initial observation, AI-assisted identification, and re-observation and validation. Data were collected through observation sheets, students' observation notes, reflective journals, group discussions, and records of AI use. Quantitative analysis revealed significant differences in observation orientations across learning phases (Friedman test, p < .001), indicating changes in observation practices over time. Qualitative findings showed that students initially relied on AI-generated cues to guide their observations. Over time, however, observation practices shifted toward direct empirical observation and peer-supported validation through repeated comparisons of plant characteristics across environmental conditions. The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from AI-reliant observation to direct observation and collaborative validation, accompanied by a gradual reduction in dependence on AI-generated outputs. These findings suggest that AI may function as an initial observational scaffold, while more sophisticated observation practices emerge through repeated engagement with phenomena and collaborative reasoning.

Purpose This systematic review analyzed 46 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, revealing eight digital technology types, including Information and Communication Technology, Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Open Educational Resources, Massive Open Online Courses, Learning Management System, and Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality. Design/Approach/Method Technologies are organized across three conceptual layers: Infrastructure, Algorithm, and Application Layer. This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. Equity outcomes prove most challenging. Originality/Value This review concludes that effective technology integration requires human-centered ecosystems that amplify, not replace, teacher agency, advancing a value-rational approach recognizing teachers’ professional flourishing as an intrinsic good rather than an instrumental means.

Using adaptive intelligence as a theoretical lens, the study investigates how L2 motivational selves are associated with AI-IDLE engagement through psychological capital (PsyCap) and L2 grit and whether these indirect associations vary with AI literacy among 1025 Chinese university EFL learners. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). For the ideal L2 self, associations with engagement emerged both directly and indirectly through PsyCap and L2 grit, whereas the ought-to L2 self showed an indirect association through PsyCap and no direct association with engagement. Higher AI literacy corresponded to stronger associations of both PsyCap and L2 grit with engagement. The two motivational self-guides were therefore associated with engagement through different psychological pathways, with AI literacy related to variation in the strength of these pathways. From an adaptive intelligence perspective, this conditional pattern indicates that the relevance of PsyCap and L2 grit to AI-IDLE engagement varies with learners’ AI literacy. These findings extend the application of adaptive intelligence to informal human–AI learning.

Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.

Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.

documents.abstract: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.

documents.abstract: This study evaluated intrinsic and extrinsic motivation determinants affecting faculty job performance and retention at Asian Institute of Computer Studies (AICS) Commonwealth, Quezon City (N=35). Using descriptive-correlational design, findings revealed very high intrinsic motivation (M=4.51 fulfillment, M=4.40 autonomy) but low extrinsic salary satisfaction (M=2.68). Regional salary disparities were identified as major push factor (M=4.11) prompting migration to public institutions, with uncertain 3-5 year retention (M=3.06). Five policy interventions are proposed: compensation restructuring, workload optimization, non-monetary pathways, facilities upgrade, and participative leadership.

Background: Artificial intelligence chatbots, particularly ChatGPT, have emerged as increasingly popular sources of health information for the general public. However, concerns persist regarding the accuracy, safety, and appropriateness of AI-generated medical advice, especially for life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction. Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT-generated responses and information to public questions about heart attacks, assess user perceptions and trust, and compare AI-generated content with expert-validated sources. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and March 2026. A total of 73 commonly asked heart attack-related questions were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-4), and responses were independently evaluated by two expert reviewers and one external reviewer using standardized rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, clarity, safety, and tone. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. In parallel, a survey of 352 participants evaluated user perceptions, trust, and behavioral use of ChatGPT for medical information. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariable regression models to identify predictors of trust and satisfaction. Results: Expert reviewers assigned high ratings for accuracy (mean: 4.62 ± 0.62 and 4.48 ± 0.63) and safety (mean: 4.78 ± 0.51 and 4.05 ± 0.50), with substantial inter-rater agreement (ICC = 0.788). In contrast, the external reviewer documented considerably lower completeness ratings (2.59 ± 0.57), revealing deficiencies in information coverage. Remarkably, 40.6% of respondents indicated they had followed ChatGPT's medical recommendations without seeking professional consultation, while 17.6% reported depending on the chatbot during urgent medical situations. Levels of user trust and satisfaction were moderate, showing significant correlations with perceived accuracy, usage frequency, and healthcare-related educational background. Conclusions: Expert assessments confirmed that ChatGPT generally provides accurate and safe cardiovascular health information; nevertheless, considerable inter-reviewer variability—especially the markedly lower completeness scores from the external evaluator—reveals significant gaps in content depth. These results indicate that ChatGPT functions more appropriately as an adjunctive educational resource rather than a replacement for professional medical consultation, emphasizing the necessity for enhanced safety mechanisms, clearer user instructions, and standardized content protocols when addressing high-stakes health topics. ChatGPT should be considered an adjunctive resource rather than a substitute for urgent professional medical assessment in suspected heart attack cases.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday epistemic practices, yet their epistemological status remains unclear. Existing debates typically oscillate between treating LLMs as epistemic agents or reducing them to mere tools. This paper argues that both views mischaracterize the core issue. Drawing on a teleological interpretation of 4E cognition and the paradigm of human–AI coevolution, it develops an alternative account that understands LLMs as components of extended epistemic capacities, most centrally the human capacity for judgment. On this view, epistemic capacities are not intrinsic properties of isolated subjects or systems, but purposive and relational achievements enacted within sociotechnical practices. LLMs do not possess epistemic agency or original normativity; rather, they reshape the conditions under which human judgment, inquiry, understanding, and justification unfold. By analyzing language, coevolutionary feedback loops, derived normativity, and epistemic autonomy, the paper shows how epistemic responsibility remains human while epistemic performance becomes technologically extended.

Maintaining cognitive load that is neither too high nor too low is key for workplace safety and efficiency. Cognitive load assessment research is often conducted in highly controlled laboratory environments that, by nature, come short of fully recreating the everyday manufacturing floors. In this feasibility study we explore the viability of adopting eye-tracker for assessing workers’ cognitive load as they complete seatbelt manufacturing assemblies in a factory workplace. Following the industrial partner’s availability, four assembly workers were selected for this feasibility study. They wore a portable Pupil Labs eye-tracker while completing seatbelt assembly tasks. Mental task demand was measured using subjective ratings. Results showed that the quality of the eye-tracking data was high in spite of the highly dynamic full-body motions required to complete assemblies. Also, no evidence was found that the presence of the eye-tracker interfered with task completion. Tasks deemed more mentally demanding were associated with greater pupil size and blink rate, a pattern consistent with laboratory research. Despite this study’s limitations, including its small sample size, these findings represent preliminary evidence for the adoption of eye-tracking metrics for conducting cognitive ergonomics assessments on factory floors.

As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support self-regulated learning (SRL), but its pedagogical value depends on whether interaction elicits learner cognition or substitutes for it. This study examined how students’ reported use of GenAI corresponded to an intended question-first coaching design, the perceived processes and tensions associated with SRL, and conditions relevant to potential scale. A qualitatively driven embedded case study utilized 31 reflective portfolios as the primary dataset, complemented by 53 survey responses and 68 weekly logs from 12 maximum-variation cases. Abductive, reflexive thematic analysis generated five themes. Question-led interaction appeared most useful when it prompted problem reframing, led to a bounded evidence-producing action, and preserved learner judgment through evaluation, modification, or rejection of AI suggestions. Benefits were qualified by role drift, generic interaction, cognitive substitution, uneven engagement, and continued need for human support. The findings support a distributed coaching-system interpretation in which AI-supported elicitation, pedagogical scaffolding, learner agency, reported AI-role configuration, and function-specific human support interact. The study does not demonstrate institutional scalability; instead, it identifies scale-relevant conditions including sustained engagement, manageable scaffolding, role boundaries, safety, learner judgment, and routes to human expertise.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence has unsettled more than the labour market. It has given rise to two related anxieties: an existential unease about human meaning, agency, and uniqueness—“AI anxiety”—and a quieter abdication of critical effort to machines, which recent works call “cognitive surrender.” The remedies most often proposed for these conditions, among them psychoeducation, regulation, engineering ethics, and therapy, leave a conspicuous gap, since none of them draws on aesthetic experience or on the making of meaning. This article, written from an engaged, applied art-history position, proceeds as a conceptual analysis rather than an empirical study. It defines “mindful art engagement” as a receptive, two-phase practice that moves from bare to informed looking, an open and contemplative looking followed by art-historically informed interpretation, sets out its boundaries, distinguishes the three constructs on which it bears (felt meaningfulness, art-historical understanding, and cognitive enrichment), and maps the existing evidence onto its components. On this basis, it advances a hypothesis that such a practice could contribute to emotion regulation and to cognitive enrichment in the age of AI, and that meaning is the point at which the two pathways meet.

In this paper, based on posthumanist theory and posthumanist linguistics, we discuss specific elaborations of the term interaction as found in linguistics and sociology, where interactivity, reciprocal awareness and agency are discussed as possible characteristics of human interaction. We problematise to what extent this is distinct from interaction between humans and machines. We bring these discussions in relation to illustrative observations on how users of ChatGPT report on their experiences with large language models, drawn from Reddit threads. We show that the concept of interaction is ‘under construction’, not only because we have new interactional partners but also because meaning-making is now intertwined with the changing and individually customised and at the same time collectivised media affordances of machine-learning technologies. Interaction is no longer perceived as typically taking place between two humans but as embedded in and distributed across time and space in large networks of speaking subjects, massive historical and ever-changing data sets, and algorithmic affordances.

Background University students face personal and academic demands that may challenge their adaptive functioning. Although intrinsic goals, need satisfaction, wellbeing, and academic engagement have been distinctively linked to academic achievement, an integrated model specifying how these constructs are structurally related and associated with students' academic outcomes is lacking. The present study addresses this gap by testing models grounded in Self-Determination Theory and previous evidence. Methods Participants were 2891 university students ( M age = 23.22 years, SD age = 5.25 years; 74.75% women) recruited across multiple Italian universities. The online survey comprised different measures, including socio-demographic items, the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale, the Aspiration Index, the SInAPSi Academic Engagement Scale, and the Mental Health Continuum-Short Form. Structural equation modeling was used to test two alternative model specifications. Starting from a more general model, progressively more parsimonious models were tested by constraining selected direct effects. The final model was selected based on comparative fit, overall model fit, parsimony, and theoretical coherence. Results The retained model specified wellbeing as antecedent to academic engagement. Within this model, basic psychological need satisfaction showed indirect links to academic achievement through wellbeing and academic engagement, while intrinsic goals were related to achievement only through academic engagement. Academic engagement emerged as the most proximal predictor of achievement, mediating the pathways from need satisfaction, intrinsic goals, and wellbeing. Conclusions These findings provide an integrated account of how satisfaction of basic psychological needs, intrinsic motivations, wellbeing, and academic engagement relate to academic achievement in university students. Our evidence supports a model in which psychological need satisfaction represents a relevant condition associated with wellbeing, intrinsic goals contribute more specifically to academic engagement, and academic engagement acts as the proximal mechanism linking these factors with academic achievement. Beyond advancing theoretical understanding, our results may inform preventive programs and interventions nurturing students' wellbeing while also promoting their academic performance.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, where evaluations usually ask whether a system is accurate on ordinary clinical data. This review asks instead what can happen when someone deliberately changes the data, instructions, or training to make a system fail, behave in hidden ways, or reveal confidential information, a field known as adversarial machine learning. We reviewed 113 publications (2018–2026) and grouped the reported threats into six categories: altering an input after training; corrupting the training examples; teaching a hidden rule triggered later; using the model to learn private information; placing malicious instructions in language or image-and-language models; and attacking models trained jointly across hospitals or devices. Laboratory studies showed that small deliberate changes to medical images could alter a diagnosis or a model's outline, corrupted training data could change what a model learned, and malicious prompts could produce unsafe medical responses. Effect sizes varied greatly across models, datasets, attacks, and test conditions. Several defenses helped in individual experiments, but no single defense was shown to work across all threats and settings; in one imaging study, attacks tailored to the tested defenses bypassed all five. The studies do not show how often these attacks occur in practice or harm patients; their value is to demonstrate possible failure modes under controlled conditions. Medical AI should therefore be evaluated both on ordinary clinical data and in clearly described, clinically plausible attack scenarios.

documents.abstract: Occupational health and safety is a mandatory component of public vocational training; however, lecture-based instruction may not sufficiently engage adult learners. This study examined the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement, with learning engagement as a mediating variable, among occupational health and safety trainees at the South Jakarta Regional Job Training Center, Indonesia. A quantitative explanatory survey was conducted with all 174 participants enrolled in the 2026 Batch 1 regular and Mobile Training Unit classes using saturated sampling. All participants completed a game-based learning session on the Wayground platform, formerly known as Quizizz. Data were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire adapted from established instruments and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The game-based learning experience had a positive and significant effect on learning engagement (β = 0.854, p < 0.001) and learning achievement (β = 0.592, p < 0.001), while learning engagement had a positive and significant effect on learning achievement (β = 0.343, p = 0.016). Learning engagement partially mediated the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement (indirect effect = 0.293, p = 0.017). The model explained 72.9% of the variance in learning engagement and 81.6% of the variance in learning achievement. Approximately one-fifth of participants reported technical barriers, primarily unstable internet connections, system lag, device limitations, and game time limits perceived as too short. The findings suggest that game-based learning activities can enhance learner engagement and perceived learning achievement in occupational health and safety training for adult vocational learners, provided that adequate technical readiness is ensured.

The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has significantly influenced second and foreign language education, particularly the teaching and learning of writing. Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can provide immediate feedback, generate ideas, suggest vocabulary, revise grammatical structures, and support learners throughout different stages of the writing process. However, the extent to which AI-assisted writing contributes to learners’ actual linguistic development remains an important research question. This conceptual paper examines the potential impact of GenAI on three central dimensions of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing performance: accuracy, complexity, and fluency (CAF). Drawing on recent research in second language writing and AI-assisted language learning, the paper analyzes the benefits and limitations of GenAI for each dimension. The literature suggests that AI-assisted writing can contribute particularly to grammatical accuracy and lexical sophistication by providing immediate corrective feedback and exposure to alternative linguistic forms. Evidence concerning syntactic complexity and writing fluency, however, is less consistent. Although learners may produce more polished and fluent-looking texts with AI assistance, this does not necessarily indicate corresponding development in their independent writing ability. The paper therefore argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends largely on how learners interact with the technology. When used as a supplementary writing assistant rather than a replacement for independent production, GenAI can support language development, learner autonomy, and reflective writing practices. The paper concludes by proposing pedagogical principles for responsible AI integration into EFL writing instruction and identifying directions for future empirical research.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in corporate reporting, where accounting policies and estimates require professional judgment. The central risk examined is not automated error but automated advocacy: a fluent, standard-referenced justification for a preferred treatment can now be obtained in seconds, making biased judgment a governance problem before it is an accounting problem. Using theory adaptation, this conceptual study integrates research on professional judgment, motivated reasoning, and automation reliance. It identifies five bias-amplification mechanisms: anchoring, automation bias, outcome-directed prompting, unverified justification, and diffusion of responsibility. It develops TRACE, a proposed framework comprising task boundary, regulatory grounding, alternative assessment, challenge and contradiction, and evidence trail. Its intended operation is illustrated using four constructed IFRS cases (IAS 8/IAS 16, IAS 36, IAS 37, IFRS 15) and a boundary-condition variant in which TRACE does not resolve the disagreement. The AI proposals are stylised illustrations, not model outputs or empirical data. GenAI appears most defensible when used to generate alternatives and challenge a preferred treatment, and least defensible when asked to select or justify a conclusion. TRACE may make AI-assisted judgments more attributable and contestable, but it has not been empirically validated and cannot guarantee unbiased outcomes.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems deployed in high-risk settings increasingly require models that support meaningful human oversight. Concept-based models (CMs) offer a promising framework by enabling users to inspect and intervene on intermediate, human-understandable concepts. However, concept interventions can counterintuitively worsen downstream predictions, a failure mode we formalise as intervention harm. We distinguish harm after all concepts have been intervened on from harm under partial interventions, the more likely practical use case. Modern CMs often achieve high accuracy by encoding, or leaking, additional task-relevant information in their intermediate concept representations. Recent work argues that such leakage can be benign with respect to intervention harm when concept representations satisfy two conditions: sufficiency and localisation. We prove that these criteria are not sufficient to guarantee that concept interventions improve downstream performance. Across controlled and real-world settings, we find that concept supervision incompleteness is associated with increased intervention harm. Importantly, optimising the model when all concepts are intervened on, a previously proposed leakage mitigation objective, reduces endpoint harm but does not reliably prevent harmful partial corrections. Hence, we introduce a complementary monotonic intervention objective that directly penalises increases in task loss along partial intervention trajectories. Combining endpoint and monotonic intervention training substantially reduces the prevalence and magnitude of partial intervention harm while preserving concept and task predictive performance.

documents.abstract: Strategic decisions made by tourism operators are often compromised by an exacerbation of negative feelings due to extenuating circumstances. One illustrative case is Donald Trump’s tariff policy, which has generated trade tensions and global uncertainty. Against this backdrop, this research explores how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) helps tourism operators in times of uncertainty by providing them with real-time assistance, while regulating their negative emotions during the decision-making process. Drawing on the appraisal tendency framework, we examine how negative emotions influence decision-makers’ temporal deferral decisions (i.e., the deferral of short-, medium-, and long-term commitments) via the threat appraisal tendency pathway. We also propose a GenAI-modulated appraisal tendency framework, integrating GenAI-driven cognitive–emotional regulation into organisational decision-making. Using three experiments, we test a triadic buffering mechanism, where GenAI-powered information filtering and cross-checking moderate the appraisal intention pathway. This research is among the first to position GenAI as an active regulator of cognition–emotion processes, offering insights into collaborative human–AI decision-making systems.

documents.abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.

documents.abstract: Human Presence Verification in the Age of Artificial Intelligence A Preliminary Scientific and Philosophical Exploration Dear Members of the International Scientific Community, This video presents a preliminary interdisciplinary reflection on one of the emerging challenges of digital communication: How can we reliably distinguish human participation from autonomous artificial intelligence in online interactions? As conversational AI systems become increasingly sophisticated, the distinction between a human-authored message, an AI-assisted communication, and a fully automated response becomes progressively less apparent. Our research proposal explores the potential of a multimodal human-presence verification framework combining several technological approaches: - Real-time visual presence verification. - Smartphone motion sensors, including accelerometers and gyroscopes. - Cryptographic device attestation. - Time-sensitive verification challenges. - Privacy-preserving certification mechanisms. The central hypothesis is that combining independent verification signals could strengthen confidence in the physical presence of a human participant. However, verifying human presence does not necessarily establish human authorship. A verified individual may subsequently delegate communication to an autonomous AI agent. This distinction represents a fundamental scientific and philosophical question. The mathematical examples presented in this preliminary work are illustrative models rather than experimentally validated findings. They are intended to support discussion and identify directions for future research. Further investigation would require controlled experiments, statistical validation, cybersecurity assessments, accessibility evaluations, and rigorous privacy analysis. Research Ethics and Transparency This project was initiated through human reflection and developed with the assistance of ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence system created by OpenAI. The human contributor directed the conceptual exploration, identified the research questions, and remains responsible for reviewing and validating the publication. AI assistance contributed to structuring the scientific discussion, formulating illustrative mathematical models, and developing the explanatory text. This collaboration is disclosed intentionally because transparency regarding human and artificial contributions is itself central to the research question. Conclusion The objective of this proposal is not to establish that machines cannot imitate humans, but to investigate how digital systems might provide meaningful, voluntary, and privacy-respecting evidence of human presence. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of communicating on our behalf, the challenge is not merely to identify who is speaking, but to understand who is present, who is responsible, and what constitutes authentic participation. We invite researchers in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital identity, philosophy, and human–computer interaction to examine, challenge, and further develop these preliminary ideas. Jean Baudrillard (2019) suggests that we are living in a hyper-reality where signs, symbols, and symptoms no longer refer to a true or real sense of reality. In other words, ‘the territory no longer precedes the map’. Such a position can be found across industry, education, and governmental communications (for example Edvardsson, Enquist and Johnston, 2005; Rose and Wood, 2005; Arvidsson and Caliandro, 2016; Hogan and Thompson, 2025) and can lead to a sense of ‘self-referential hyperauthenticity’. This hyperauthenticity runs counter to the Higher Education valued benchmarks of quality and standards that rely upon a human externality of critical experience. This chapter will critique some of the current literature regarding the ‘hype’ and ‘overhype’ of an artificial intelligence integrated future (Thais, 2024; Marr, 2025) and present imagined directions for the reassurance of all Higher Education’s stakeholders: including government, society, HEI’s, and most importantly its students. Such a positive vision of the future is critical to balance against what could be considered a commercially speculative dream, and rather than dreaming of electric sheep its users inhabit a world where the opportunities of AI enhance the learning in and of our human experience for the benefit of society as a whole. A series of AI future narrative case studies will be critiqued against Baudrillard’s theory of hyper-reality and balanced with a new reading of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs (Montag et al, 2025). This places human well-being at the centre of the experience and will reveal how the simulacrum of an AI future is yet to be proven with any empirical evidence (Marr, 2025). The chapter is consciously presented to educators and assessment designers through authentic assessment principles (see Brown and Sampbell, 2023, and Herrington, Reeves, and Oliver 2009) to demonstrate how a broader definition of authenticity in assessment can include AI and work alongside the values of the high quality further and higher education. Drawing from empirical analyses of AI functions and capabilities, and aligning with meaningful authentic learning and assessment principals (Ajjawi et al., 2023; McArthur, 2023) and case studies, a modest narrative will be proposed with some futureproofing speculations. These are aimed at fundamentally empowering the agency of Higher Education Institutes. It will show and how we might hold AI as a powerful tool of human educational development, and how we might create a connected future with a human hand inside a digital glove that will ultimately inform the public, protect student’s interests, and maintain high-quality education provision (Quality Code, 2024).

documents.abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.

Saudi Arabia’s industrial expansion under Vision 2030 increases the strategic importance of preventing loss of containment across oil and gas, petrochemical, water, utilities, and infrastructure assets. This review examines how health, safety, and environment (HSE) governance can be integrated with intelligent leakage detection so that sensing technologies become part of accountable risk management rather than isolated technical tools. An integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published during 2020–2025 synthesizes evidence on acoustic sensing, pressure and flow analytics, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), machine and deep learning, digital twins, risk-based inspection, dynamic risk analysis, human factors, and safety governance. The synthesis shows that intelligent systems can improve detection speed, localization, and predictive integrity assessment, but technical accuracy alone does not ensure safer outcomes. Governance quality determines whether alerts are validated, escalated, translated into barrier actions, documented, and learned from. The paper proposes an HSE-integrated architecture linking sensor assurance, contextual analytics, dynamic risk ranking, human authorization, emergency response, maintenance, and sustainability metrics. It argues that Saudi industrial operators should treat leakage intelligence as a safety-critical decision system with defined ownership, cybersecurity controls, model assurance, and lifecycle verification. Research priorities include Saudi field datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, cross-asset interoperability, human–AI decision protocols, and evidence connecting intelligent detection to measurable reductions in environmental releases and major-accident risk.

Introduction Independent music practice depends on learners’ self-regulated learning (SRL), yet how digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) support the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of the SRL cycle, and when such support may undermine learner autonomy, remains unclear. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO through March 2026. Sixteen empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Because of methodological heterogeneity, we conducted a thematic synthesis rather than a meta-analysis. Results Three categories emerged: traditional digital tools, discriminative AI, and generative AI. Traditional tools supported planning and reflection; discriminative AI enabled real-time error detection; and generative AI may help learners manage task difficulty and translate expert feedback into actionable steps. Study quality was uneven, and several findings came from small-sample or cross-sectional designs, which limits causal inference. Two potential risks, over-scaffolding that may diminish autonomy and visual feedback that may divert attention from sound, were insufficiently studied. Discussion Digital and AI tools appear to scaffold different phases of SRL, but learner autonomy should remain at the core. Fading explicit support and pedagogical guidance may help reduce dependence. Longitudinal studies are required to test these mechanisms.
